keyVerseText: And the children of Israel said unto him, We will go by the high way: and if I and my cattle drink of thy water, then I will pay for it: I will only, without doing any thing else, go through on my feet.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מֶכֶר (meker) derives from the root מָכַר (mâkar), which fundamentally means 'to sell' or 'to give over.' This root conveys the act of transferring ownership, whether literally selling goods or figuratively surrendering oneself. The noun מֶכֶר therefore captures the concept of 'price' or 'merchandise'—the object or value exchanged in a transaction. This etymology enriches the common English gloss by emphasizing not just the item or value itself but its role as something given in exchange or as a measure of worth.
usageInScripture: The word מֶכֶר appears three times in Scripture, consistently relating to the idea of value or merchandise. It is translated variously as 'all manner of ware' and 'for her price,' showing its application both to commercial goods and to intrinsic worth, such as the value of a capable woman. This range demonstrates that מֶכֶר encompasses both tangible goods and abstract value, highlighting the concept of price as both a physical and moral measure.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מֶכֶר as 'price' or 'merchandise' rooted in the act of selling deepens our grasp of biblical themes of redemption and sacrifice. It reminds us that much in Scripture involves the idea of exchange—God's people are bought or redeemed at a price, pointing ultimately to Christ's atoning work. The concept of value inherent in מֶכֶר challenges believers to consider what is truly precious in God's sight. It also calls attention to the costliness of grace and the seriousness of surrendering oneself to God, reflecting the root meaning of 'to sell' or 'to give over.'
keyVerseReflection: In Numbers 20:19, the Israelites offer to pay for water, saying, 'if I and my cattle drink of thy water, then I will pay for it.' Here, מֶכֶר underscores the principle of just compensation and respect for property. The use of this word highlights the seriousness of the transaction and the recognition of value even in something as basic as water. It teaches a biblical ethic of fairness and integrity, reminding believers that all resources have worth and that honoring others' possessions aligns with God's justice.
